title: Ines and the Hidden Ledger
markdown:
The air in Fuentepiedra hung thick with figs and the slower smell of money that had not been collected. Ines Duarte, daughter of Lord Silvanus, moved through the house like a person who had been given rooms instead of a life. Her father's frown could curdle milk. He had given her a task that sat in the bones: retrieve a ledger, taken by persons no one would name, that chronicled every coin owed to the crown. Magistrate El Supremo, whose belly preceded him like a walking mountain, had declared the family's honour imperilled.

"You must, Ines," Silvanus boomed, "or face the Magistrate's displeasure."

She longed, with a child's leftover wish, to sprout wings.

Far from tax offices, at the shadowed confluence of two forgotten rivers, Mateo Cruz smuggled not silk but knowledge. His spectacles glinted like captured starlight while he traced a worn map salvaged from a crumbling monastery. He knew ancient treaties and forgotten decrees better than any king's scribe. Ines had heard the hushed tales. She went to him because she had nowhere else that was not a cage.

Fog clung to the riverbank. Mateo stepped from behind a moss-covered boulder.

"Ines Duarte," he said, calm as a man reciting a date. "You seek the misplaced ledger."

She nodded. Her hands were not steady. "Stolen. Magistrate El Supremo demands its return."

Mateo adjusted his spectacles. "Ah. The Magistrate. He collects taxes with the zeal of a magpie hoarding trinkets, and a similar disregard for their origin." The chuckle was dry, like pages. "The rogues who took it are likely heading for the old Roman road, the one through Serpent's Pass. Few know its hidden shortcuts. I do."

They mounted a travel-worn donkey named Sancho and left as if the hour itself were being taxed. The Magistrate's guards, stout men in ill-fitting uniforms, scoured the main routes, voices like ill-tempered giants. Mateo veered onto a track that was barely a rumour.

"A Roman legionary path." He pointed to faint indentations in the stone. "They built for permanence, not for the fleeting whims of overzealous collectors."

Ines clung to Sancho's mane. Wind whipped her hair and brought wild thyme. For a mile or two she was not a daughter with a commission. She was simply going.

A glint of metal. Figures with overflowing sacks tried the narrow gorge on a rickety rope bridge.

"Never trust a bridge that appears to have been recently chewed by goats," Mateo murmured. He indicated a stabler goat track winding down. "The ledger is not merely stolen. It is being delivered to someone who understands its true value."

They descended. The guards floundered behind, armour a hindrance, shouting at a bridge that did not care.

At the gorge's bottom they found not bandits but a lone scholar, face etched with the particular worry of a man who has been trusted with paper. A royal archivist.

"The ledger!" he exclaimed. "It contains King Alfonso's decree."

The decree was older than El Supremo's appetite. Taxes could never exceed twenty percent of a farmer's yield. The Magistrate, in his avarice, had been taking nearly double. The so-called thieves were royal agents, trying to keep the parchment from a fire the Magistrate would have called housekeeping.

Ines took the ledger. The leather was worn, the ink still sure. She did not make a speech about courage. She held the thing as if it might argue if she dropped it.

They raced back to Fuentepiedra and arrived as El Supremo was loudly berating a pale Lord Silvanus for the missing accounts. Ines stepped forward. Her heart was a drum. Her voice, when it came, was clear.

"Magistrate. I believe these papers belong to the crown. And they tell a most revealing story."

She read the decree aloud in the dusty hall. El Supremo's face turned a shade of purple rarely seen outside bruised plums. A clerk, who had spent years pretending not to hear percentages, stopped pretending.

The Magistrate was stripped of his title. Parchment had done what shouting could not. Ines stood in the same hall that had made her small and found it had not grown; she had simply stopped whispering. Mateo Cruz nodded once, a private victory, spectacles catching the high window. Sancho, outside, ate someone's uncollected fig. The ledger lay open on the table, twenty percent looking, for the first time in years, like a number and not a rumour.
characters: Ines Duarte (tax farmer's daughter), Mateo Cruz (smuggler historian)
